drove the business planning of the administration and is the basis for the budget in front of you today.
In order to do this, the 2019 Business Plan and Budget followed a four step process.
Step one was to develop the city's baseline and the cost to maintain existing service levels.
Step two was to use that information and develop an indicative property tax target to help guide the rest of the process.
Step three involved the development of business plans to achieve city council priorities within the targeted property tax.
And step four is the reviews. City Council is about to undertake today and the next few days to incorporate the business plan into the overall budget.
Going into a little bit more detail in each one of the steps.

The first step to determine the cost to maintain existing service levels started with an internal review of departmental and divisional budget requests that focused on revenue and expenditure estimates based on inflation and civic growth components only.
There were no service level increases considered during this time.
Departments and divisions were given a zero percent expenditure increase as a starting point.
And everyone was asked to review and justify their internal budget, which was subsequently reviewed by internal budget team consisting of the general managers city manager and finance staff.
Through this process, as Mr. Jordan said,

Approximately four million dollars in targeted continuous improvement reductions was returned to divisions and departments with the expectation they find a more efficient way to deliver their services.
Once the internal process was finished, the city was left with approximately $10.6 million in inflationary impacts or 1.82% increase over 2018 for civic services.
The city's common metric to measure inflation pressure is MPI or the municipal price index, which is currently estimated at 1.93% for 2019.
In addition, 6.9 million in growth expenditures were identified in order to maintain existing services.
This is the result of expanding roadways, sidewalks, and park service areas, as well as other factors such as growing population.
To illustrate some of the growth pressures included in the 2019 budget, nearly 78 kilometers of roadways was added in 2018 that will have an operational impact in 2019.
This is a result in an additional budget pressures for services such as Saskatoon Transit, snow removal, and the city's building better road program to name a few.
In addition, 69 hectares of increase in green space are estimated to be added in 2018 that will have an operating impact in 2019.
This is a direct impact on the city's expenditures for parks maintenance, playground maintenance, and other parks and recreation programs.
On the revenue side, the city was estimated $10.2 million in additional revenue, which comes from four main sources.
User fees, external funding, internal funding, and of course the property tax.

User fees are remaining relatively flat in 2019, as increases to programs such as the Saskatoon Forestry Farm, parking services, and leisure centers are offset by decreases in revenues from transit and parking violations.

The city is expecting an increase of approximately 7 million in 2019 from internal and external sources, largely as a result of the reinstated Sask energy franchise fee, as well as the continued phase in of the Saskatoon water return on investment.
The city was also expecting $3 million in assessment growth, which has recently been finalized at $2.85 million.
The administration is recommending using the previously held contingency to offset this decrease, which is included in the business plan option, reports within the agenda.

So overall, utilizing the city's funding gap formula in order to maintain existing services, a $7.3 million gap has been identified, which translates into the 3.16% property tax increase mentioned by Mr. Jordanson.
Step two of this process was presented to the governance and priorities committee in May 2018, which outlined options for targeted property tax outside of simply maintaining existing services.

Options included targeting a property tax increase of less than 3.16%, which would require the identification of service level changes, new revenues, or a further adjustment to user rate fees than what's presented today.
The other option included was a rate higher than 3.16, which would allow for implementation of initiatives and projects aimed at achieving city council strategic priorities.
As a result of the May 2019 GPC meeting, a targeted property tax increase was identified at 4 to 4.5%.
The third step involved identification and prioritization of which initiatives to fit within the targeted property tax while still achieving city council priorities.
This process was presented to the June 2018 GPC, where nearly $8 million in options were presented.
As a result of this meeting, 2.6 million was set aside for business plan options initiatives while 500,000 was placed into a contingency to provide funding for further unforeseen changes in risks.
Throughout the summer committee prioritized these initiatives via an online survey of which the results were presented to the August 20th GPC meeting.
The administration has further refined the listing and the final recommendation is included in the business plan options report, which is included in the year agenda as item 6.14.
Step 4 is where we're at today. Going back to the funding gap equation, there is now 10.4 million.
There's now a 10.4 million funding gap identified once the business plan options and contingency are taken into account.
This translates into the 4.5% property tax increase included within year agenda.
On an overall basis, the 2019 proposed business plan and budget totals approximately $1.14 billion, which is similar to the 2018 budget approved budget considered a year ago today.
The largest portion of the operating expenditures continues to go to Saskatoon Police Service, Transportation, Recreation and Fire, which make up nearly 56% of the city's total expenditures.

The city's largest expenditure item continues to be staff compensation, coming in at nearly 58% of total expenditures, followed by operating costs such as contractors, materials, supplies, fuel and utilities at 24% and transfers to reserve at 12% of the overall budget.
The largest source of funding to balance the business plan and budget continues to be property taxation, coming in at 48% of all funding.
While general revenues account for nearly 20% which is made up of sass to known utilities return on investment, interest earnings, franchise fees and finds and penalties to name a few.
The city's 2019 proposed capital budget is nearly $260 million, a decrease of $36 million over the 2018 approved capital budget.
The largest capital programs continue to be the land development program at $71 million, utilities at $69 million and transportation at $60 million.
Some of the more significant projects aside from the city's land development and utilities program are just over $31 million for the city's building better roads program.
Over $14 million for continued work on the growth plan to half a million and bus rapid transit.
$13.5 million for the city buck walled bridge repairs and $5 million for the Gordie House Sport Complex City contribution.
It's important to note that the city's 2019 proposed budget does not include any new borrowing, but does include the following repayments based on the existing debt today.
$23 million in repayments from the property tax, $10.5 million in repayments from gas tax, and $9.5 million supported by utility rates.
